title: The Work of Our Hands
subtitle: A five-session study on work and vocation, and the faith that has to survive Monday.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has sat in a pew on Sunday feeling that their faith was real and large, and then walked into a job on Monday where it seemed to shrink to nothing. It is for the believer who suspects, somewhere underneath, that the real work of God happens on a stage with a microphone and that their own forty hours at a desk or a register or a job site are spiritually beside the point. It walks slowly through five movements on what work is and was meant to be, on Eden where God himself worked and called it good, on the thorns and the sweat that came after, on the lie that splits the world into sacred jobs and secular ones, on the idol that work becomes when it stops being what we do and starts being who we are, and on the strange promise that our labor is not finally lost. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that will tell you to find your passion and the rest will take care of itself, because most work is not passion and most weeks are not inspired, and the gospel has something to say to the ordinary Tuesday and not only to the calling that thrills you. It refuses two lies at once. The first says ordinary work does not matter to God, that only ministry counts, and the study takes that lie apart with Luther and Dorothy Sayers and the whole doctrine of vocation. The second says work is everything, the place we earn our worth and prove we exist, and the study names that as the idol it is. Most of all the study implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He is a pastor, and the pastorate is a job, a job he has loved into an idol, a job he has hidden behind, a job whose busyness he has called faithfulness when it was really fear. He has made the work of God a way of avoiding God. He writes from inside the problem. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Before the Thorns
sessions.aim: To recover the truth the church keeps forgetting, that work is older than sin, given in the garden before anything broke, part of the good creation and the image of a God who himself works, and not the punishment we secretly believe it is.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell, after a long week, that he could not wait for heaven so he would finally never have to work again. It was said as a joke, and it was not a joke. Underneath it sat a belief most Christians hold without ever examining it, that work is a curse, a consequence of the fall, a thing God imposed when Adam sinned and a thing we will be rid of when we are saved. The first question of this whole study is whether that is even true, and it is not. Open Genesis and the first worker in the Bible is God. He labors over six days and calls the labor good, and then he makes a creature in his image and the very first thing he gives that creature is a job. Work the garden. Keep it. Name the animals. This is before the serpent, before the fruit, before the thorns. Bell takes the strong form of the view that work is a curse, that Scripture plainly says cursed is the ground and by the sweat of your face you will eat, and grants that something did go wrong with work. But the curse fell on work that already existed. It did not invent work. Work is part of Eden, not part of the fall. To be made in the image of a working God is to be made to work, to make, to cultivate, to bring order out of raw material the way he did. Then the turn. If work is part of the good creation, then the believer who despises all work as a necessary evil is not being spiritual. He is being unbiblical, mourning a curse where God gave a gift, and missing the dignity God stitched into the work of his own hands.

keyScripture.why: The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden to work it and keep it, placing a job in human hands before a single thing had gone wrong, which means work belongs to the good creation and not to the fall, and dignifies labor as part of what it means to bear the image of a God who works.

discussion.q: Before tonight, did you privately think of work as a blessing, a curse, or just a necessary evil you put up with to pay for the parts of life that actually matter?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before correcting anything. Most people in the room carry an unexamined verdict on their own work, and it is usually a low one, a thing endured rather than received. The point is not to settle it yet but to expose the assumption. Land it on honesty, not consensus. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: The first worker in the Bible is God, laboring over six days and calling it good. What does it do to your view of your own job to start there, with work as a divine activity rather than a human punishment?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the curse reflex. We assume work began when things went wrong. The aim is to notice that God worked before any creature did, and called the working good, so that labor is dignified at the root. Help them feel the weight of being made in the image of a God who makes.

discussion.q: God gave Adam a job, to work the garden and keep it, before the fall, before anything broke. Why do you think the church so often talks as if work itself were the problem rather than what the fall did to work?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Keep it off abstract theology and on the lived assumption. We mourn a curse where God gave a gift. Help the room see that despising all work as a necessary evil is not a spiritual posture but an unbiblical one, a failure to read past chapter three.

discussion.q: To be made in the image of a working God is to be made to make, to cultivate, to bring order out of raw material. Where in your own work, however ordinary, have you felt that flicker of being made for this?
discussion.behind: Move from doctrine to recognition. You are not hunting for people with glamorous jobs. The accountant bringing order to chaos, the parent making a home out of raw days, the welder joining what was apart, all of it is image-bearing. Help even the weary find the dignity buried in their week. Go first.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has treated his own work as the thing standing between him and the life he really wanted. Where have you done the same, living for the weekend or the retirement, as if the work itself were the enemy?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication. You are not adding guilt, you are exposing a quiet despair most of us carry, that the bulk of our waking hours is a thing to be survived. The gospel reaches our Mondays only after we admit how little we expected God to be there. Go first.

objections.objection: Work is obviously a curse. Genesis says it plainly, cursed is the ground because of you, by the sweat of your face you will eat. The Bible itself calls work a consequence of sin, so do not dress it up as a gift.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it. Something did go wrong with work, and Genesis names it without flinching, the thorns, the sweat, the futility, all of it real and all of it the result of the fall. We will spend the whole next session inside that curse, because the study refuses to pretend Monday does not hurt. But read more carefully where the curse falls. It falls on work that was already there. Adam was working the garden in chapter two, before the serpent says a word, given the job by God himself and called to it as part of what it meant to bear God's image. The curse did not create work. It corrupted work that the Creator had already given and already called good. To say work is a curse is to confuse the wound with the thing that was wounded. Work is Eden's gift. The thorns are the fall's vandalism of the gift, and the difference is the whole point.

objections.objection: If work is so good and so much a part of God's design, why does the Bible end with rest, with a Sabbath, with no more curse and no more toil? Heaven is the end of work, which proves work was never the point.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because there is real truth in it. Scripture does end with rest, and the toil and the futility, the cursed parts of work, are gone forever, and that is a mercy worth longing for. But look closely at what the end of the Bible actually pictures, because it is not an eternity of idleness. The city has builders. The kingdom has servants who reign and serve. The new creation is described with the language of cultivation and offering, the nations bringing their glory in. What ends is not work but the curse on work, the sweat and the thorn and the sense that it is all for nothing. The rest of God is not the absence of all activity. It is the end of striving and futility, work finally freed to be what Eden meant it to be. Heaven is not the abolition of work. It is its redemption, and we will arrive there in session five.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the work you do most of your waking hours, and when did you last let yourself believe that God was in it and pleased with it, rather than waiting for you somewhere else?
sessions.practice: This week, pick one ordinary task in your work, the most routine thing you do, and before you begin it, say out loud that this is part of how you bear the image of a God who works. Then do it with attention, as if it mattered, because it does. At the end of the week, write down whether naming the dignity of the task changed how it felt to do it, even a little, even once.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you worked before any of us did, and you called the working good, and then you made us in your image and put work into our hands as a gift before anything had broken. Forgive us for despising what you blessed, for treating the better part of our lives as a sentence to be served. Teach us to see our labor the way you saw your own over those six days, as good, as ours, as a way we are like you. Meet us in the garden of the ordinary, in the work of our hands, and let us find you there. Amen.
reflection: Where have I called work a curse when God called it good, and what would change if I read my own week as part of the image I bear rather than the punishment I serve?
When I imagine the life I really want, is it a life with no work in it, and what does that reveal about what I think work is for?
If God gave Adam a job before the fall, what does that say about whether my ordinary labor matters to God right now, today, before I get anywhere better?
sessions.teaching: Start where the trouble starts, with a man who said something he did not know he believed. After a long week he told me, half laughing, that he could not wait for heaven so that he would finally never have to work again. We both laughed. And then I could not stop thinking about it, because underneath the joke sat a conviction that almost every Christian I know carries without ever once examining it. Work is a curse. It is the thing God hung on us when Adam sinned, the price of the fall, the burden we will finally lay down when we are saved. Heaven, in this picture, is the great vacation, the end of the alarm clock, the eternal Saturday. And if that is true, then the bulk of our waking lives, the forty or fifty or sixty hours a week most of us spend at our labor, is a kind of holy waiting room, a thing to be endured until the real life begins. So before we go anywhere else in this study, we have to ask whether it is even true. It is not. Open the Bible to its first page and watch who the first worker is. It is not Adam. It is God. In the beginning God creates, and the language of Genesis one is the language of labor, of a craftsman over a workbench, separating and forming and filling and ordering, six days of work, and at the end of each day he steps back and inspects what he has made and calls it good. The first thing the Bible tells you about God is that he works, and that his work is good. This matters more than we let it. Because then God makes a creature in his own image, and the very first thing he does with that creature, before the fall, before the serpent, before a single thing has gone wrong, is give him a job. The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden to work it and to keep it. Adam is a gardener before he is anything else. He names the animals, which is the work of a scientist and a poet at once. He is given a world of raw material and told to cultivate it, to bring order and beauty and fruitfulness out of it, the way his Maker brought a cosmos out of the formless deep. Work, in other words, is in Eden. It is part of the original good. It is woven into what it means to be human and to bear the image of a God who himself works. Now take the objection at full strength, because it is the honest one and the text is right there. Does not Genesis say, cursed is the ground because of you, in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life, by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. Yes. It says exactly that, and we will spend the whole next session inside those words, because the study has no interest in pretending that Monday does not hurt. Something did go wrong with work. The thorns are real. But look at where the curse lands. It lands on work that already existed. The sweat and the futility are not the invention of work. They are the corruption of a work that God had already given and already called good two chapters earlier. The fall did not create labor. It vandalized labor. It took a gift and drove thorns through it. And so to call work itself a curse is to make a mistake as basic as confusing a wound with the body that was wounded, as confusing the graffiti with the wall. Work is the wall. Sin is the graffiti. They are not the same thing, and the entire question of how a Christian should think about Monday turns on telling them apart. Here is the verdict, and the leader has to hold it cleanly through everything that comes after. Work is not the curse. Work is the gift the curse fell on. To be made in the image of a working God is to be made to work, to make, to build, to grow, to bring order out of chaos, and a believer who despises all labor as a necessary evil to be escaped is not being more spiritual than the rest of us. He is being less biblical. He is mourning a gift and calling the mourning faith. And I have to stand inside this, because I have done it for years. I have treated my own work, even the work of ministry, as the thing standing between me and the life I actually wanted, living for the day off and the study leave and the eventual rest, as though God were waiting for me somewhere on the far side of my labor instead of present in the middle of it. The man who joked about never working again was only saying out loud what I had been believing in silence. So we begin by going back before the thorns, to the garden where God worked and called it good, and put a job in human hands, and pronounced the whole arrangement, the worker and the work together, very good. That is where your Monday actually comes from. Not from the fall. From the goodness of God.

scriptureStudy.note: In the beginning God created. The first thing Scripture tells us about God is that he works, and the verb is the verb of a maker. Before any human labors, the divine worker is already at the bench, which means work is godlike before it is ever burdensome.

God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. The Creator inspects his finished labor and pronounces it good, the way a craftsman steps back from the bench. Work is dignified at the root because God himself worked and was pleased with the result.

On the seventh day God finished his work, and he rested. Even the rest is defined in terms of work, rest from labor completed, not idleness. The rhythm of work and rest is built into creation before sin ever enters.

The Lord God put the man in the garden to work it and keep it. The first command to the first human is a job, given in Eden, before the fall. Work is the original assignment, not the consequence of sin.

God brought the animals to the man to see what he would call them. Naming is the work of ordering and understanding the world, intellectual and creative labor handed to the image-bearer as part of his calling, all of it before anything breaks.

Be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion. The first blessing on humanity is a commission to cultivate and steward the creation, a mandate to work the world, given as a blessing and not a burden.

You have given him dominion over the works of your hands, you have put all things under his feet. The psalmist sees human work as a delegated share in God's own rule over creation, dignifying the laborer as a steward and not a slave.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long argument the church has had with itself about whether work is noble or base, because the assumption that labor is beneath the truly spiritual life is older than any of us and has done real damage. In much of the ancient world, manual work was the lot of slaves and the lower orders, and the contemplative life of the mind was held to be higher, a hierarchy the church partly absorbed, so that for long stretches the monk at prayer was thought to be doing holier work than the farmer in the field, and the priest at the altar holier work than the woman at the loom. There was a real insight buried in it, the recognition that not all of life reduces to production, that the soul has a vocation beyond the paycheck. But it hardened into a lie, the splitting of the world into a sacred tier of work that counts to God and a secular tier that does not, a lie this study takes apart fully in session three. Set that against the witness of Genesis, where God works and the first human is a laborer and the dignity of work is established before any priest or temple exists. A serious group should weigh both the wisdom and the error in the older view, honoring the truth that we are more than what we produce while rejecting the falsehood that ordinary labor is spiritually second-class. Lester DeKoster, in his small book Work, argues that work is the form in which we make ourselves useful to others, and so a primary way we love our neighbor, a claim worth holding up against any theology that treats the daily grind as beneath God's notice. The aim is to recover what Eden established and the church too often forgot, that the God who worked has dignified the work of our hands.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in the congregation, raising three children at home, told Bell she had stopped saying what she did when people asked, because the answer just a mom always landed like an apology. She had sat through years of sermons celebrating people who left their careers for the mission field and felt, every time, that her own days of laundry and meals and the slow shaping of small souls were the part of life God was waiting out. Walk the group through her week with the eyes of Genesis. She is bringing order out of chaos, cultivating, making a home out of raw days, doing the work of an image-bearer in the most literal sense, raising the next generation the way Eden's first command pointed toward. Ask the group where they, like her, have apologized for ordinary work that God himself dignified. The point is not to flatter her, but to help everyone see that the gift of work in the garden reaches all the way down into the unglamorous and unpaid labor most of us actually do.

memoryVerse.text: The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.

sessions.title: Thorns and Sweat
sessions.aim: To tell the honest truth about why Monday feels the way it does, to name the curse on work without explaining it away, and to refuse both the lie that good work is always satisfying and the despair that says it is all for nothing.
sessions.summary: If work was a gift, why does so much of it feel like punishment. That is the question session two will not dodge. The same Genesis that puts a job in human hands before the fall tells us, after the fall, that the ground is cursed, that thorns and thistles will come up, that we will eat by the sweat of our faces all the days of our lives. The first thing to see is that the curse is not on the worker but on the work, on the ground itself, so that the same task now resists the hand that does it. Work that flowed becomes work that fights back. Bell takes the strong form of the cynic, who says this is just the way of all flesh, that work is meaningless toil, that Ecclesiastes is right and it is all vanity and a chasing after wind. He grants the weight of it, because Scripture itself grants it. The Preacher really does say that he hated all his toil, that the worker leaves it all to someone who did not labor for it. The futility is in the Bible. But the curse is not the original word and it is not the final one. It is the middle of the story, the long, hard middle most of us live in, between the garden where work was good and the new creation where work will be good again. Then the turn. Naming the thorns honestly is itself a mercy, because the believer who has been told that good Christian work should always feel meaningful and fulfilling is being set up to despair the first ordinary, grinding, thankless Tuesday. The curse explains the grind. And a faith that cannot account for the grind is a faith that will not survive Monday.

keyScripture.why: Cursed is the ground because of you, in pain you shall eat of it, thorns and thistles it shall bring forth, by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, naming the corruption of work after the fall as a curse on the ground itself, so that labor now resists the laborer, and giving honest language for why Monday feels the way it does.

discussion.q: If work was a gift in the garden, why do you think so much of your own work feels like a grind, a thing you push through rather than a thing you delight in?
discussion.behind: Open on the lived experience before the doctrine. Let the room be honest about how heavy work can feel without rushing to fix it. The aim is to surface the gap between the good gift of session one and the actual Monday, because that gap is exactly what the curse explains.

discussion.q: The curse in Genesis falls on the ground, not on the worker. Thorns come up to resist the hand that works. How does it land to hear that the resistance you feel in your work is the world being broken, not you failing at it?
discussion.behind: Land the key distinction. Many people read their frustration at work as personal inadequacy. The aim is to relocate the problem from the worker to the cursed ground, which is both more honest and more freeing, without letting anyone use it as an excuse to stop trying.

discussion.q: Bell takes the cynic's view seriously, that work is just vanity and chasing after wind, the way Ecclesiastes says. What is true in that, and what does it miss about where the curse sits in the whole story?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Ecclesiastes really does name the futility, and the room should not leave thinking the Bible is naive about meaningless toil. The miss is treating the curse as the first word and the last word, when it is the middle. Help them locate the grind between Eden and the new creation.

discussion.q: Where have you secretly believed that if your work were the right work, it would always feel meaningful, and what has that belief done to you on the ordinary, thankless days?
discussion.behind: This is the convicting center. The culture sells a gospel of passion and fulfilling work, and it sets believers up to despair when most weeks are not inspired. Press gently on the lie that good work should always feel good, and how it makes the normal grind feel like proof something is wrong.

discussion.q: Bell admits there are mornings he has resented even the work he was called to, ministry itself, and has had to drag himself to it like a man pulling thorns. Where have you resented your own work, and what would it mean to name that without shame?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. The point is permission, not confession-hunting. Even good and called work can feel like sweat and thorns, and naming that honestly is healthier than pretending. Go first, and keep it gentle. The aim is to let people stop performing satisfaction they do not feel.

objections.objection: Work is just meaningless toil. Ecclesiastes is right, it is all vanity, you labor your whole life and then leave it to someone who did not earn it and will waste it. There is no dignity in the grind, only the grind.
objections.response: Bell grants the weight of this and does not win cheaply, because Scripture itself grants it. The Preacher in Ecclesiastes really does say he hated all his toil under the sun, that the wise man dies like the fool, that the worker leaves his labor to one who comes after and may be a fool. The futility is in the Bible, named without flinching, and any honest faith has to reckon with it. But notice where the futility sits in the larger story. It is not the first word about work, which was good, and it is not the last, which is the new creation. It is the curse, the long middle, the broken stretch we actually live in. Ecclesiastes is telling the truth about work under the sun, work cut off from God, work as the only thing. It is not telling the whole truth about work under the gaze of a Creator who gave it and a Redeemer who will not let it be lost. The vanity is real. It is just not final.

objections.objection: So the answer is that work is supposed to be miserable, and I should just accept the misery as my lot. If the curse explains the grind, then I should expect nothing better and stop hoping work could be good.
objections.response: No, and the study is careful here, because the curse is an explanation, not a sentence to passivity. Naming that the ground is cursed does not mean we bless the thorns and stop pulling them. The whole calling of work after the fall is to push back against the curse, to bring order where there is chaos, to make things grow where the ground resists, which is itself a small participation in the redemption God is working. The curse explains why work fights back. It does not tell you to surrender to it. And it does not mean work is now only misery, because grace breaks into the middle of the story, and there are real satisfactions, real goods, real moments where the gift of Eden flickers through even now. The curse accounts for the grind so that you do not despair when it comes. It does not require you to stop hoping, or stop laboring, for the good that work was meant to be.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the part of your work that feels most like pulling thorns, the resistance you push against week after week, and have you ever told anyone how heavy it actually is?
sessions.practice: This week, when the resistance comes, the thankless task, the thing that fights back, do not call it your failure and do not pretend it does not weigh on you. Name it for what it is, out loud or on paper, the ground resisting the hand, the curse and not your inadequacy. Then do the work anyway, as one pushing back against the thorns. Write down whether naming it honestly changed how you carried it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you gave us work as a gift, and then the world broke, and now the ground itself resists the hand that works it, and we have carried that resistance as if it were our own failure. We are tired. Some of us dread the morning. Forgive us for the lie that good work should always feel good, and forgive us for the despair that says it is all for nothing. You have not abandoned us to the thorns. You entered them, you wore them on your head, and you are redeeming even our hardest labor. Meet us in the sweat of our weeks, and give us the strength to keep pulling thorns until the curse is lifted for good. Amen.
reflection: Where have I read the resistance in my work as proof that I am failing, when it may be the broken world fighting back, and what would change if I named it as the curse and not my inadequacy?
Have I been quietly waiting for work that finally feels meaningful all the time, and what has that done to me on the ordinary, grinding days?
What does it mean that the curse is the middle of the story and not the end, and how would my Monday feel different if I really believed the thorns were temporary?
sessions.teaching: We ended last week in the garden, with work as a gift, with a God who labored and called it good and put a job in human hands before anything broke. And if we stopped there, the study would be a lie, because none of us live in chapter two. We live in chapter three and everything after, and chapter three is where the thorns come in. So this week we have to be honest, more honest than the church usually is, about why work that was a gift so often feels like a punishment. If work is good, why does Monday feel the way it does. Genesis does not dodge the question, and neither will we. After the man and the woman eat, God speaks the consequences, and listen to where the curse on work actually falls. Cursed is the ground because of you. Not cursed are you. Cursed is the ground. In pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life, thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. See the precision of it. The curse does not land on the worker. It lands on the material the worker works with. The ground itself is now set against the hand that tills it. The same labor that flowed in the garden now fights back. Thorns come up where you planted wheat. The harvest fails for reasons you cannot control. The project collapses after months of effort. The customer is cruel, the boss is a fool, the body breaks down, the spreadsheet will not balance, the children you are raising push against every good thing you try to plant in them. This is not work being abolished. It is work being frustrated, work made to resist, so that what was pure gift now comes mixed with sweat. And here is something pastoral and freeing buried in the grammar. The resistance you feel in your work is not first of all evidence that you are bad at it. It is evidence that the world is broken. The thorns are not your inadequacy. They are the curse. Now take the cynic at full strength, because his voice is in the Bible itself, and any faith that cannot face him is too thin to bother with. The Preacher of Ecclesiastes looks at all of it and says it is vanity, a chasing after wind. He says he hated all his toil under the sun, because he would have to leave it to the one who came after him, and who knows whether that man will be wise or a fool. He says the worker labors and the fool inherits, that the wise man dies the same as the fool, that there is nothing new and nothing lasts. This is in your Bible. The futility of work is named there, flatly, without comfort, and we must not pretend otherwise or wave it off with a verse. There are days, there are seasons, there are whole careers, where work feels exactly like this, like rolling a stone uphill only to watch it roll back down, like building what will be torn down, like pouring yourself into what no one will remember. Grant it. The vanity is real. But now ask where the futility sits in the whole story, because the cynic has made one mistake. He has treated the curse as the first word and the last word, when in fact it is the middle. The first word about work was good, the gift of Eden. The last word about work, as we will see, is redemption, our labor caught up into the new creation and not lost. The vanity Ecclesiastes describes is the truth about work under the sun, work severed from God, work as the only thing there is. It is not the whole truth about work under the gaze of the God who gave it and the Christ who is redeeming it. The vanity is real. It is simply not final. And this is exactly why naming the thorns honestly is not pessimism but mercy. Because here is what happens to the believer who has never been told this. He has absorbed, from the culture and sometimes from the church, the gospel of fulfilling work, the lie that if you find the right job, your true calling, your passion, then work will be deeply satisfying all the time, and the satisfaction will be the proof that you are where God wants you. And then he gets the actual job, and most of it is ordinary, and some of it is tedious, and a great deal of it is thankless, and the first grinding, joyless Tuesday hits him like a verdict. Something must be wrong. Wrong job. Wrong calling. Wrong with me. And he is set up to despair, or to quit, or to keep restlessly chasing the work that will finally feel the way the lie promised, which does not exist. The doctrine of the curse rescues him. It tells him the grind is not a sign he is in the wrong place. The grind is the condition of all work this side of Eden, the thorns coming up in every field, and the right job will have them too. A faith that cannot account for the grind is a faith that will not survive Monday. And I have to confess that I live in the thorns as much as anyone, and that I have resented even the work I was most sure God called me to. There are mornings I have dragged myself to the work of ministry like a man pulling weeds, mornings I have stood to preach with no fire in me, weeks where the calling felt like sweat and nothing else. I have hidden that, because pastors are supposed to be above it, which is its own kind of lie. So let me say it plainly, so you can say it too. The thorns are real, even in good work, even in called work. Your dread on a Monday is not proof your faith has failed. It is proof you are working cursed ground, like every other child of Adam. But we do not pull thorns forever. Christ wore them on his head, and the day is coming when the ground will be free. Until then we work the broken field, honestly, without the lie that it should feel like Eden, and without the despair that says it is only vanity. The curse is the middle of the story. We do not live at the end yet. But we know how it ends.

scriptureStudy.note: Cursed is the ground because of you, in pain you shall eat of it. The curse falls on the ground, the material of work, not on the worker himself, so that labor now resists the laborer. The frustration of work is the world broken, not the soul failing.

Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth, by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. Work now comes mixed with sweat and resistance, the gift corrupted but not destroyed. This is the honest account of why even good work fights back.

I considered all that my hands had done, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind. The Preacher names the futility of work under the sun without comfort, and Scripture lets the complaint stand, because a faith that cannot face the vanity is too thin to trust.

I hated all my toil, because I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool. The dread that our work will be wasted by those who inherit it is named honestly here, the curse felt as the fear that nothing lasts.

The creation was subjected to futility, in hope that it will be set free from its bondage to corruption. Paul names the same futility Ecclesiastes felt, but locates it in a story with an ending, a creation groaning toward freedom and not abandoned to the thorns.

When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength. Spoken to Cain, the words show the curse on work deepening with sin, the ground withholding its strength, the laborer estranged from the fruit of his labor.

And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head. The very symbol of the curse on work, the thorn, is pressed onto the head of Christ, who takes the curse into himself, the first sign that the thorns will not have the last word.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the honest tradition of lament about work that runs through Scripture and the church, because a faith that only celebrates work and never grieves its frustration is not the faith of the Bible. Ecclesiastes is the great example, a book the church has often been embarrassed by, because it refuses easy comfort and stares at the vanity of toil without blinking, yet it sits in the canon precisely because God's people need permission to say the work feels meaningless sometimes. Set this beside the modern condition, where the culture has swung to the opposite error, preaching that work should be your passion and your identity and the source of your meaning, a gospel of fulfilling labor that crushes the ordinary worker the moment the work turns dull or hard. A serious group should weigh both errors, the cynicism that says work is only vanity and the romanticism that says work should always thrill, and ask which one has more quietly shaped them. Tim Keller, in Every Good Endeavor, names this directly, writing about the simultaneous dignity and futility of work, that work is both noble in its design and frustrated by the fall, and that the Christian holds both at once rather than collapsing into either the cynic's despair or the romantic's disappointment. The discipline this session requires is to learn the lost art of lament over work, to say honestly that the grind is real and heavy, while refusing the lie that the grind is the whole truth, because the same God who let Ecclesiastes into the Bible also promised that our labor in him is not in vain.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in the group had spent eleven years building a small business, pouring his evenings and his savings into it, only to watch it fail in a single bad year he could not have prevented. He came to the study quietly convinced the failure was a verdict, that if he had been more faithful or more gifted or more blessed by God the thing would have stood. Use his story to test the doctrine of the curse. Ask the group whether the ground sometimes resists the hand no matter how good the hand is, whether thorns come up in fields that were planted right. The aim is to help him hear that the collapse of honest work is not always a referendum on the worker, that the curse means even diligent labor can come to nothing through no sin of the laborer, and that Ecclesiastes named this grief long before he felt it. Then ask the harder thing. Where is the line between the curse he could not control and the choices he could, and how does honesty about both keep him from either false guilt or false innocence. Let the group sit in the tension without resolving it too quickly.

memoryVerse.text: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken.

sessions.title: The Lie That Splits the World
sessions.aim: To kill the lie that ministry is holy work and everything else is secular and second-class, to recover the priesthood of all vocations, and to hear from Luther and Dorothy Sayers that the work of the milkmaid and the carpenter pleases God as fully as the work of the priest.
sessions.summary: There is a lie so deep in the church that most believers do not even know they hold it. The lie says that some work is sacred and some work is secular, that the pastor and the missionary do God's work while the plumber and the accountant merely do their jobs, and that the closer your work is to a church building the more it counts to God. Session three takes that lie apart. The first thing to see is that Scripture knows no such division. Bell takes the strong form of the view that ministry really is more important, that surely preaching the gospel matters more than fixing a sink, and grants there is something true in it, that the eternal weight of the gospel is real. But the conclusion does not follow, because God does not need a special religious category of work to be pleased. He is pleased by the milkmaid who milks to his glory as surely as by the preacher who preaches to it. This is Luther's great recovery, that vocation is not a churchly word but a creation word, that God calls the farmer and the magistrate and the mother as truly as he calls the priest, and that God himself is milking the cow through the milkmaid, feeding the world through the labor of ordinary hands. Dorothy Sayers drives it home, asking why no one ever thinks to teach a carpenter that the very first demand of his religion is that he make good tables. Then the turn, and it cuts toward the pastor first. If all honest work is holy, then the pastor's work is not more holy, only differently assigned, and the moment a minister thinks his collar makes his labor count more to God than the labor of the woman cleaning the church, he has joined the very lie the gospel came to destroy.

keyScripture.why: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, addressed not to priests but to ordinary workers, even slaves, refusing any division between sacred and secular labor and making every honest task an offering to God, so that the work of the most ordinary hands is done unto the Lord himself.

discussion.q: Be honest. Somewhere underneath, have you believed that a pastor or a missionary is doing more important work for God than you are at your ordinary job? Where did that belief come from?
discussion.behind: Surface the lie before naming it. Most people in the room carry the sacred-secular split without examining it, and it makes them feel their daily work is spiritually beside the point. The aim is to bring the buried assumption into the open so it can be challenged. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Luther said God himself is milking the cow through the milkmaid, feeding the world through her ordinary hands. What changes when you picture God working through your job to care for your neighbors, rather than waiting for you at church?
discussion.behind: Land Luther's image. We imagine God present in religious work and absent from secular work. The aim is to relocate God into the ordinary task, so the believer sees their labor as the means by which God himself provides for the world, which dignifies the dullest job.

discussion.q: Dorothy Sayers asked why no one teaches a carpenter that the first demand of his faith is to make good tables. Where has your faith stayed in the spiritual part of your life and never reached the actual quality and ethics of your daily work?
discussion.behind: Press on the gap Sayers names. Many separate their faith from their craft, as if God cared about their devotional life but not their workmanship. The aim is to connect faith directly to the excellence and integrity of the work itself, the good table as a matter of religion.

discussion.q: If all honest work is holy to God, what does that do to the way you have ranked jobs, including your own, as more or less spiritual? What might change in how you treat people in unglamorous work?
discussion.behind: Move from self to neighbor. The lie not only diminishes our own work but lets us look down on others. The aim is to dismantle the ranking entirely, so the room honors the janitor and the nurse and the farmer as doing work God values, and stops envying the platform jobs.

discussion.q: Bell confesses that as a pastor he has secretly believed his work counted more to God, that the collar made his labor holier than the labor of the people in his church. Where do you sort your own life into work that counts and work that does not?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, and note that Bell turns the knife on himself, the professional Christian. Everyone ranks their hours into the meaningful and the meaningless. Invite the room to find where they do it, and go first. The point is to end the ranking, in the leader's heart first.

objections.objection: Surely ministry really is more important than secular work. Preaching the gospel deals with eternity, and fixing a sink does not. You cannot seriously claim a plumber's work matters to God as much as a missionary's.
objections.response: Bell grants the half that is true, because the eternal weight of the gospel is real and the study will not pretend otherwise. The proclamation of the gospel does deal with eternal things, and it would be foolish to flatten every difference between tasks. But the conclusion does not follow, and here is why. The question is not which work has the most visible eternal content. The question is what pleases God, and God is pleased by obedience and love offered through honest labor, whatever the labor is. He does not need a special religious category to be glorified. The plumber who fixes the sink so a family has clean water, done unto the Lord and in love of that neighbor, is doing work God receives as fully as the missionary's sermon. Luther saw this, that God milks the cow through the milkmaid and rules through the magistrate and heals through the physician, all of it his work done through ordinary hands. The gospel is supreme in its message. It does not create a caste system of holy and unholy jobs.

objections.objection: If every job is equally holy, then why does it matter what I do at all? This just lets people stay in selfish, even harmful work and call it their calling. It erases any real difference between vocations.
objections.response: No, and the doctrine of vocation has a sharp edge here that the study keeps. Saying all honest work is holy does not mean all work is honest. The con artist, the predatory lender, the maker of what destroys his neighbor, these have no vocation in the Christian sense, because vocation is defined by love of neighbor, by work that serves and does not exploit. Lester DeKoster argued that work is the way we make ourselves useful to others, so work that harms rather than serves fails the very test of vocation. And within honest work, the doctrine does not erase the difference between doing the job well and doing it badly, faithfully and corruptly. What it erases is the false ranking of jobs by their proximity to a church building. It dignifies the honest plumber. It does not bless the dishonest one, and it presses every worker, in every field, toward the love of neighbor and the integrity that make the work an offering God can receive.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you truly believed God was working through your ordinary job to love your neighbors and provide for the world, what is the one thing you would do differently at work tomorrow?
sessions.practice: This week, take the work you have most quietly considered unspiritual, the most ordinary part of your job, and do it as Sayers said, aiming to make a good table. Whatever your version of a good table is, the well-kept books, the clean room, the patient phone call, the careful repair, do that one thing with the deliberate intention that the excellence of it is an offering to God and a love of your neighbor. Write down whether treating the craft itself as worship changed the work.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you milk the cow through the milkmaid and feed the world through the work of ordinary hands, and we have insulted you by dividing our days into the holy hours and the secular ones, as if you were present only in church. Forgive us for ranking your callings, for envying the platform and despising the bench. Forgive those of us in the work of ministry most of all, for the pride that made our labor count more in our own eyes than the labor of your people. Teach us that all honest work done unto you is holy, and send us back to our jobs as priests of the ordinary, to make good tables to your glory. Amen.
reflection: Where have I divided my life into work that counts to God and work that does not, and what would it mean to offer the whole of it to him as one undivided thing?
If God is working through my job to provide for my neighbors, who exactly are the neighbors my work serves, and have I ever seen my labor as love for them?
Whose work have I quietly looked down on as less spiritual than my own, and what does that ranking reveal about the lie I have absorbed?
sessions.teaching: There is a lie buried so deep in the soil of the church that most believers have never once dug it up to look at it, and it is quietly poisoning the way they think about the forty hours that fill their week. The lie is this. Some work is sacred and some work is secular. The pastor, the missionary, the worship leader, the seminary professor, these people do the work of God. The plumber, the accountant, the line cook, the schoolteacher, the stay-at-home parent, these people do mere jobs. And the closer your work sits to a church building or a Bible, the more it counts to God, while the further out it sits, into the ordinary economy of the world, the more it shrinks to something God merely tolerates while he waits for you to come back inside and do the real thing on Sunday. If you have ever felt that your job was spiritually beside the point, that the actual mission of God was happening somewhere else and you were just funding it, you have felt the weight of this lie. So we are going to take it out and break it. Start with Scripture, because Scripture simply does not know this division. When Paul writes to the Colossians, whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, he is not writing to clergy. He is writing to ordinary believers, and the very next breath is addressed to slaves, to people doing the most menial labor imaginable, and he tells them that their work, their work, is done for the Lord Christ himself and that from him they will receive their reward. There is no asterisk. No footnote that says except for the dull jobs, the secular jobs, the ones that do not feel religious. Whatever you do. The whole of the daily grind is swept up and handed back to the worker as an offering made directly to God. Now take the objection at its strongest, because it is the one every serious Christian feels. Surely ministry is more important. Preaching the gospel touches eternity. Fixing a sink does not. How can you possibly say the plumber's work matters to God as much as the missionary's. And there is something true here that the study refuses to flatten, the eternal weight of the gospel is real, and not every task carries the same visible eternal content. Grant it. But watch the conclusion fail to follow. The question is not which job has the most obvious religious content. The question is what pleases God, and what pleases God is obedience and love offered up through honest work, whatever the work happens to be. God does not need a special sacred category in order to be glorified by your Tuesday. This is Martin Luther's great recovery, and the church has been forgetting it ever since he said it. Luther took the word vocation, which the medieval church had reserved for the calling to be a monk or a priest or a nun, the so-called religious life, and he blew it wide open. Vocation, he said, is not a churchly word. It is a creation word. God calls the farmer to farm and the magistrate to govern and the mother to mother and the cobbler to cobble, and these are callings every bit as holy as the call to preach. And then Luther says the thing that should rearrange how you see your Monday. When the milkmaid milks the cow, he said, it is God who is milking the cow through her. God feeds the world. But he does not rain bread down from the sky. He feeds the world through the farmer who grows the grain and the baker who bakes it and the trucker who hauls it and the cashier who sells it. God himself is at work in the milkmaid's hands. Your job, however ordinary, is one of the ways the providing hand of God reaches into the world to care for your neighbors. You are not on the sidelines of the work of God. You are the means of it. Dorothy Sayers put the same truth to a sharper edge in her essay Why Work, and her question should sting every one of us. She asked why it is that the church will fuss over a carpenter's church attendance and his private morals and never once think to tell him that the very first demand his religion makes on him is that he make good tables. Good tables. The integrity and the excellence of the work itself, she argued, is a matter of religion, not a separate secular thing happening alongside his faith. A carpenter serves God by carpentry, by making a table that is true and strong and well-joined, and a Christian carpenter who makes shoddy tables while keeping his devotions has missed the point entirely. The work is the worship. Or it is meant to be. And now the turn, and I have to take it standing in the place it cuts deepest, because I am the professional Christian here, the man with the collar, the one this lie flatters most. If all honest work is holy, then the work of the pastor is not more holy than the work of the people in the pews. It is differently assigned, not more valuable. And I will confess to you that I have not always believed that in my bones. I have stood up here and quietly felt that what I do, the preaching and the praying and the counseling, counts to God in a way that the labor of the woman who cleans this building after we leave does not. That is the lie, in its purest and ugliest form, wearing a clerical collar. The gospel did not come to build a caste system of sacred and secular jobs with the clergy on top. The gospel came to tear that wall down, to make every believer a priest and every honest task an altar. The moment I think my work matters more to God because it happens in a church, I have rejoined the very lie that Christ died to kill. So hear it, all of you, and let it reach the place where you have been ranking your hours. There is no secular work for the Christian, only work done with God or without him. The milkmaid and the missionary, the carpenter and the cleric, the spreadsheet and the sermon, all of it, done heartily as for the Lord, is holy. Go make good tables.

scriptureStudy.note: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. Addressed to ordinary workers and slaves, not clergy, this refuses any sacred-secular split and makes all honest labor an offering to Christ himself.

Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. The glory of God is not confined to religious acts but extends to the whole of ordinary life, including the most mundane, so no part of work falls outside the reach of worship.

I have filled Bezalel with the Spirit of God, with skill in every craft, to work in gold and silver and bronze. The first person Scripture says is filled with the Spirit is not a prophet but a craftsman, and the filling is for excellent artistic work, dignifying skilled labor as Spirit-empowered.

You are a royal priesthood. The priesthood belongs to all believers, not a clerical class, which means every Christian offers their whole life, including their work, as priestly service, and no honest vocation is spiritually second-class.

Let each person lead the life the Lord has assigned to him. Paul roots vocation in God's assignment, so the ordinary station and the ordinary job are themselves the place of calling, not a holding pattern until something more spiritual comes along.

Bondservants, render service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man. Even the most ordinary and constrained labor is reframed as service rendered to Christ, who receives the work directly, regardless of how secular the task appears.

The Lord was with Joseph, and his master saw that the Lord caused all that he did to succeed in his hand. Joseph serves God through faithful, excellent work in a secular household, and God is present and at work in that ordinary labor, not only in the temple.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the history of how the church split the world in two, because the sacred-secular divide did not fall from heaven, it was built over centuries and it can be dismantled. In the medieval period a sharp line was drawn between the so-called religious life, the monks and nuns and clergy who were thought to have a true vocation, a calling from God, and the laity in their ordinary trades, who were merely permitted their lower station while the spiritual elite pursued the higher way. The word vocation itself was reserved for the cloister. Martin Luther shattered this in the Reformation, insisting that the plowman and the milkmaid and the magistrate have callings as genuine as any monk, that God works through the ordinary stations of life to govern and provide for the world, a teaching the doctrine of vocation has carried ever since. Set this beside the modern secular version of the same split, where work is divided into the meaningful careers that supposedly express your true self and the mere jobs you endure for money, a new caste system that crushes the worker in ordinary labor just as the old one did. A serious group should weigh both the medieval and the modern divisions and ask how deeply each has shaped them. Os Guinness, in The Call, distinguishes the primary calling, to God himself, from the secondary callings, to our particular work and stations, warning against both collapsing all of life into work and dismissing ordinary work as spiritually empty. Gene Veith's work on Luther and vocation, and Dorothy Sayers's essay Why Work, are the sharpest tools for this session. The aim is to recover what the Reformation recovered, that there is no sacred caste of jobs, only the whole of honest labor offered to the one Lord.
sessions.caseStudy: Two people in the same group, on the same week, named their work. The first was a young woman headed to the mission field, and the room lit up, prayed over her, took up a collection. The second was a man who installs heating systems, and when he said it the room nodded politely and moved on. He noticed. He always notices. Use the contrast as the case study. Ask the group, gently and directly, why the room responded the way it did, and what the difference reveals about the lie they have all absorbed. Then walk the heating installer's work through the doctrine of vocation. In a Michigan winter, he is the reason families do not freeze, the hand through which God himself keeps the vulnerable warm, doing the love of neighbor in copper and flame. His work is no less holy than the missionary's, only differently assigned. The aim is not to diminish the missionary but to lift the installer, and to make the room repent of a ranking they did not even know they were keeping. End by asking each person whose ordinary work they have quietly counted as lesser.
